title: Classical-witness hierarchy contained in the mixed-state quantum hierarchy
formal: Is the quantum-classical polynomial hierarchy contained in the quantum polynomial hierarchy with unentangled mixed-state proofs? The precise historical target is \[\mathrm{QCPH}\subseteq\mathrm{QPH}.\] Both hierarchies use constantly many alternating quantifiers followed by a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier, with an inverse-polynomial acceptance gap. QCPH quantifies over classical strings; QPH quantifies over density matrices whose joint input to the verifier is their tensor product. The number of quantifiers may increase by a constant factor in the containment. Grewal and Yirka’s CCC2024 Theorem26 gives an affirmative answer, even with a constant gap in the resulting QPH protocol.

why: This establishes that alternating mixed quantum certificates can express every problem obtained by alternating classical certificates before quantum verification. It supplies a basic comparison between two natural hierarchies while preserving the distinctions among classical, mixed, pure and entangled proof models.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Grewal–Yirka, CCC2024 Theorem26. sentences: The historical question compares alternating classical certificates with alternating unentangled mixed quantum certificates.
It asks whether every promise problem in QCPH also belongs to some fixed level of QPH.
The presence of universal quantifiers makes this more subtle than replacing one classical certificate by a quantum state.
Grewal and Yirka prove the containment with a constant acceptance gap and a constant-factor increase in the number of quantifiers.
The original source itself acknowledges that concurrent result, so the completed card is archived as resolved.

definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. Let \(n=|x|\). No correctness condition applies outside the promise. Fix an integer level \(i\ge1\) and a polynomial witness-length bound \(p(n)\). Let \(Q_j=\exists\) for odd \(j\) and \(Q_j=\forall\) for even \(j\); \(\overline Q_j\) denotes the other quantifier. Completeness and soundness thresholds \(c(n),s(n)\in[0,1]\) are polynomial-time computable rational functions of the input length, with \(c(n)-s(n)\ge1/q(n)\) for some fixed positive polynomial \(q\). These thresholds and resource bounds may depend on the promise problem and level, but not on the particular input.

A uniform quantum verifier is specified by one deterministic classical polynomial-time algorithm that, on input \(1^n\), outputs a circuit \(V_n\). It acts on the classical input \(x\), the \(i\) proof registers of \(p(n)\) qubits each and polynomially many zero-state ancillas, with polynomially many gates. One designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; value one means accept. Use the concrete universal gates \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two and \(i\) in \(e^{i\pi/4}\) is the imaginary unit. Gates act as identity on other wires. Fixed-gate synthesis errors may be absorbed into the inverse-polynomial gap with polynomial overhead; no perfect-completeness convention is being imposed.

For classical proof strings \(y_j\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), let \(a_x(y_1,\ldots,y_i)\) be the verifier's acceptance probability when each proof is encoded as the corresponding computational-basis state. The promise pair lies in \(\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_i(c,s)\) when \[x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\Rightarrow Q_1y_1\cdots Q_iy_i:\ a_x(y_1,\ldots,y_i)\ge c(n),\] \[x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\Rightarrow\overline Q_1y_1\cdots\overline Q_iy_i:\ a_x(y_1,\ldots,y_i)\le s(n).\] Quantifiers range over all strings of the stated length. Each later choice may depend on earlier choices. An individual tuple need not yield probability outside the interval \((s(n),c(n))\); only the displayed alternating conditions are promised. Let \(\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_i\) be the union over the allowed thresholds and resources.

For the mixed-state analogue, every proof variable \(\rho_j\) ranges over all density matrices on \(p(n)\) qubits. A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho_j=\rho_j^\dagger\), \(v^\dagger\rho_jv\ge0\) for every complex vector \(v\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho_j=1\). There is no finite-description or efficient-preparation requirement on these states. The verifier receives \(\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_i\), with no entanglement between proof registers. Each register may have internal entanglement and may be mixed. If \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output one and \(a\) is the ancilla count, define \[b_x(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_i)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_n\bigl(|x\rangle\langle x|\otimes\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_i\otimes|0^a\rangle\langle0^a|\bigr)V_n^\dagger\right].\] Membership in \(\mathrm Q\Sigma_i(c,s)\) replaces every classical variable in the two preceding quantified conditions by \(\rho_j\), and \(a_x\) by \(b_x\). Again take the union over inverse-polynomial gaps to define \(\mathrm Q\Sigma_i\). This is the mixed-state, unentangled hierarchy; it is not the pure-state restriction or the variant permitting entanglement across quantified registers. The alternating quantifiers express mathematical dependence on previously chosen states, not a physical protocol required to learn an unknown quantum state from one copy.

Set both zeroth levels to BQP, the promise problems decided by a uniform polynomial-time quantum circuit without witnesses and with acceptance thresholds \(2/3,1/3\). Define \[\mathrm{QCPH}=\bigcup_{i\ge0}\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_i,\qquad \mathrm{QPH}=\bigcup_{i\ge0}\mathrm Q\Sigma_i.\] Each problem uses some fixed finite level; the level cannot grow with input length. Containment means that every promise pair in the first union belongs to some level of the second, possibly with a different verifier and polynomial proof length. It does not require \(\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_i\subseteq\mathrm Q\Sigma_i\) at the same level. The resolution paper defines its unnamed QPH levels with a union over constant gaps; its theorem for that smaller collection also proves the inverse-polynomial-gap target stated here. No general error-reduction theorem for mixed-state QPH is assumed.
answer_criterion: The mathematical target is a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{QCPH}\subseteq\mathrm{QPH}\) under the quantified promise definitions above. A theorem producing a constant-gap mixed-state protocol at a larger constant level suffices. The published CCC2024 Theorem26 resolves this historical question and is the reason for archival; the present review does not supply or certify a Lean formalization. Containment only in the pure-state hierarchy or in a hierarchy allowing entangled proof registers would concern a different class. Equality of the two hierarchies, a same-level containment and arbitrary amplification of the mixed-state hierarchy are stronger assertions not requested here.

context_blocks.text: The imported excerpt says that the authors did not know how to prove QCPH contained in QPH. A later concurrent-work paragraph in the same paper records that Grewal and Yirka proved exactly that inclusion, with a constant-factor increase in hierarchy level. The shortened import missed this resolution already acknowledged by its source.

A quantum proof can be measured to obtain a classical string, but this observation alone does not transfer an alternating proof system. A later quantified choice can depend on a classical string; if an earlier quantum proof generates a distribution of strings, the later choice cannot simply know the eventual measurement outcome. This explains why the inclusion needs a theorem.

The original paper proves inclusion in a hierarchy with pure quantum proofs. The selected question concerns mixed proofs instead. Alternating maximization and minimization prevent the usual one-witness convexity argument from identifying those models automatically.

CCC2024 Theorem26 proves PH contained in QCPH contained in QPH. Section5 gives the proof and explicit acceptance bounds. Its output has a constant gap; known amplification of the classical-proof verifier handles every inverse-polynomial input gap. A constant increase in the number of quantifiers remains inside the union defining the hierarchy.

The resolution paper’s title concerns a separate entangled hierarchy, whose levels do collapse. Its QCPH-to-QPH theorem instead concerns unentangled mixed-state proofs. The two results should not be conflated, and the inclusion does not imply equality or collapse of the unentangled hierarchy.
